processing: Black tea made at the estate's own factory, sold plain or flavoured, with vanilla the best-known option. The method details are little documented.
harvest_season: Prized pickings are not documented; the tea is sold as a year-round product.
appearance_dry: Dark, fine leaf, as is usual for a packaged black tea of this kind.
appearance_liquor: Clear reddish brown, typical of a plain black tea.
appearance_wet: Small coppery-brown leaf, as expected of this type.
taste_profile: Few independent notes exist for the plain tea, which should be a simple everyday black tea; the vanilla version adds the sweet aroma its name promises.

brewing.notes: A general starting point for a small-leaf black tea. Flavoured versions go flat if oversteeped.

vintage_note: Sold year-round as a packaged tea, with no vintage. Flavoured lines (vanilla, bergamot, mint, coconut, lemon) lose their aroma first, so buy them recent and keep them sealed.
description:
Bois Cheri is the best-known name in Mauritian tea, a plantation and factory in the south of the island. It is often described as the country's largest tea producer, and most people meet it on the island's tea route.

It makes black tea, plain and flavoured, along with newer green and herbal lines. The method details are little documented, so think of it as a straightforward packaged tea.

The flavoured teas are the local signature, vanilla most of all. Drink the plain tea for what it is, an everyday cup, and keep steeps short with the flavoured ones.

You can buy it easily on the island. The factory tour with a tasting is worth doing, and mornings are said to be the time to see the machinery running.
history:
The estate is generally dated to 1892, when it began producing tea. It is linked to the first large-scale tea growing on the island, though the early details vary from one account to another.

The site now runs a small museum with old machinery and 19th-century tea sets, and it is a stop on the Mauritian tea route along with the colonial house at Domaine des Aubineaux.
